title: Library Imports and Setup
content: Imports Mathlib for equivalences (bijections on $\mathbb{N}$), monotonicity, and tactics. The `abbrev Perm := \mathbb{N} \equiv \mathbb{N}$` encodes permutations as bijections.
mathContext: A permutation $\pi: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is formalized as `Perm := ℕ ≃ ℕ`, an equivalence type ensuring bijectivity. `Logic.Equiv.Basic` provides the $\equiv$ type and `Order.Monotone.Basic` provides `StrictMono`/`StrictAnti` for index monotonicity.

title: Arithmetic Progressions (3, 4, 5-term)
content: Defines $k$-term APs via constant difference: IsAP3$(a,b,c)$: $b-a = c-b$ with $a < b < c$. IsAP4 adds a fourth term, IsAP5 extends to five. These are the core combinatorial objects.
mathContext: IsAP4$(a,b,c,d)$: $b - a = c - b = d - c$ with $a < b < c < d$. The common difference $d = b - a$ determines the AP. IsAP5$(a,b,c,d,e)$: IsAP4$(a,b,c,d) \wedge d - c = e - d \wedge d < e$.

title: Monotone $k$-APs in Permutations
content: HasMonotone$k$AP$(\pi)$ requires indices $i_1, \ldots, i_k$ that are either all increasing or all decreasing, with values $\pi(i_1), \ldots, \pi(i_k)$ forming a $k$-AP. The monotonicity of indices distinguishes this from APs in arbitrary subsequences.
mathContext: HasMonotone4AP$(\pi)$: $\exists i < j < k < l$ (or $i > j > k > l$) with IsAP4$(\pi(i), \pi(j), \pi(k), \pi(l))$. The index monotonicity means the AP values appear in natural reading order (left-to-right or right-to-left) in the permutation sequence.

title: Erdős Problem 196 — The Open Conjecture
content: Every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ contains a monotone 4-term AP. This sits at the critical threshold: $k = 3$ is proved and $k = 5$ is disproved. The conjecture has resisted all approaches since 1977.
mathContext: erdos_196_conjecture: $\forall \pi: \mathbb{N} \equiv \mathbb{N},$ HasMonotone4AP$(\pi)$. Axiomatized as the open problem. The gap between $k = 3$ (forced) and $k = 5$ (avoidable) makes $k = 4$ a sharp threshold question.

title: DEGS Theorem: $k = 3$ Always Exists
content: Davis, Entringer, Graham, and Simmons (1977) proved that every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ contains a monotone 3-term AP. The proof uses a compactness argument: any infinite permutation contains arbitrarily long monotone subsequences, and among three consecutive terms of a monotone subsequence, one finds a 3-AP.
mathContext: degs_3ap_theorem: $\forall \pi: \mathbb{N} \equiv \mathbb{N},$ HasMonotone3AP$(\pi)$. This follows from the infinite Ramsey theorem or by direct pigeonhole on residues modulo the common difference.

title: DEGS Construction: $k = 5$ Avoidable
content: DEGS (1977) constructed an explicit permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ avoiding all monotone 5-term APs. The construction interleaves blocks of integers in a pattern that breaks any potential 5-AP while preserving the bijection property.
mathContext: degs_5ap_counterexample: $\exists \pi: \mathbb{N} \equiv \mathbb{N}, \neg$HasMonotone5AP$(\pi)$. The construction is recursive: partition $\mathbb{N}$ into blocks and permute within/between blocks to prevent 5-term monotone APs.

title: 4-AP Conjecture Implies 3-AP Theorem
content: If every permutation has a monotone 4-AP, then every permutation has a monotone 3-AP. Proved by extracting three terms from the 4-AP. This is a non-trivial Lean proof using `omega` for the arithmetic.
mathContext: conjecture_implies_3ap: $(\forall \pi,$ HasMonotone4AP$(\pi)) \implies \forall \pi,$ HasMonotone3AP$(\pi)$. Given indices $i < j < k < l$ with IsAP4$(\pi(i), \pi(j), \pi(k), \pi(l))$, take the first three to get IsAP3$(\pi(i), \pi(j), \pi(k))$.

title: Odd and Even Common Difference
content: A 4-AP has odd (resp. even) common difference if $(b - a) \bmod 2 = 1$ (resp. $0$). This parity distinction is the key structural reduction discovered by LeSaulnier and Vijay.
mathContext: IsAP4OddCD$(a,b,c,d)$: IsAP4$(a,b,c,d) \wedge (b - a) \bmod 2 = 1$. IsAP4EvenCD$(a,b,c,d)$: IsAP4$(a,b,c,d) \wedge (b - a) \bmod 2 = 0$. Every 4-AP falls into exactly one category.

title: LeSaulnier–Vijay: Odd-CD 4-APs Avoidable
content: LeSaulnier and Vijay (2011) constructed a permutation avoiding all monotone 4-APs with odd common difference. This dramatically narrows the open problem: to prove the conjecture, one need only show that even-CD 4-APs cannot be avoided.
mathContext: lesaulnier_vijay_odd_avoidable: $\exists \pi, \neg\exists i < j < k < l:$ IsAP4OddCD$(\pi(i), \pi(j), \pi(k), \pi(l))$. The construction separates odd and even integers in a careful pattern that disrupts odd-CD APs.

title: Parity Dichotomy
content: Every 4-AP has either odd or even common difference. Combined with LeSaulnier–Vijay, this shows the conjecture reduces to forcing even-CD 4-APs. Proved by case analysis on $(b-a) \bmod 2$.
mathContext: ap4_parity: IsAP4$(a,b,c,d) \implies$ IsAP4OddCD$(a,b,c,d) \lor$ IsAP4EvenCD$(a,b,c,d)$. Proved by `by_cases hp : (b - a) % 2 = 1`. This is a constructive proof in Lean using `omega`.

title: Equivalence to Even-CD Forcing
content: The conjecture is equivalent to: every permutation avoiding odd-CD monotone 4-APs must contain an even-CD monotone 4-AP. This structural reduction is the deepest known simplification of the problem.
mathContext: conjecture_equiv_even_forced: $(\forall \pi,$ HasMonotone4AP$(\pi)) \iff \forall \pi, (\neg\exists$ odd-CD 4-AP$) \implies \exists$ even-CD 4-AP. The backward direction is the heart of the equivalence: if odd-CD 4-APs can be avoided, even-CD 4-APs must compensate.

title: Non-Extendability Constraint
content: If a permutation avoids monotone 4-APs, then every 3-AP $(\pi(i), \pi(j), \pi(k))$ is non-extendable: the value $\pi(k) + d$ (where $d$ is the common difference) cannot appear at any later monotone index.
mathContext: non_extendable_constraint: $\neg$HasMonotone4AP$(\pi) \implies \forall i < j < k$ with IsAP3$(\pi(i), \pi(j), \pi(k)), \forall l > k: \pi(l) \neq \pi(k) + (\pi(j) - \pi(i))$. Each 3-AP forbids one value at all future positions, creating cumulative constraints.

title: Erdős–Szekeres Theorem
content: Every sequence of $(r-1)(s-1)+1$ distinct numbers contains a monotone increasing subsequence of length $r$ or a monotone decreasing one of length $s$. This guarantees long monotone subsequences but gives no control over arithmetic progression structure.
mathContext: erdos_szekeres: $n > (r-1)(s-1) \implies \forall$ injective seq$: \text{Fin}\,n \to \mathbb{N}$, $\exists$ StrictMono indices of length $r$ with StrictMono(seq $\circ$ indices) or StrictAnti indices of length $s$ with StrictAnti(seq $\circ$ indices).
